vignette:
He is a 55-year-old Middle Eastern man who has spent most of his life working the same land his father once worked. Before the assault, his days are steady and physical: waking before sunrise, checking irrigation lines, walking the rows, lifting feed, repairing fences with hands that rarely rest. He is known in his family as dependable and quiet, a man who does not complain and who measures himself by what he can provide. He lives with his wife, and although their children are grown, the rhythm of family life still centers around shared meals, visits, and the farm’s demands.

The assault happens at the end of a long day during harvest season. He is loading equipment into a truck when two men approach him near the edge of his property. At first he thinks they are there to ask for something or settle some dispute, but the interaction turns quickly. One of them shoves him hard, and then both men begin hitting him. He remembers the shock more than the pain at first—the confusion of suddenly being on the ground, the taste of dirt in his mouth, boots near his face, a blunt blow to his ribs, someone yelling. He tries to shield his head with his arms and cannot catch his breath. What stays with him afterward is not only the violence but the helplessness of it, the humiliating certainty in those moments that he might be killed on his own land and no one would come in time.

In the days after, he tells himself he is lucky to be alive. He says little about what happened. His wife notices the bruising, the stiffness in his movements, the way he winces getting out of bed, but she also notices something less visible. He startles when the gate slams. He checks the locks repeatedly before sleeping. At night he lies awake listening for engines, footsteps, dogs barking in the distance. When he does fall asleep, he jerks awake sweating, his heart pounding, with the sensation that someone is standing over him. Sometimes in the dream he is back on the ground, unable to move his arms quickly enough. Sometimes there is no clear image, only terror and the certainty that something terrible is happening again.

He returns to work because the farm does not wait. Animals need feeding, irrigation needs tending, crops spoil if neglected. But the work that once anchors him now exposes him. He avoids the far edge of the property where the assault took place, sending hired help or delaying tasks until absolutely necessary. If he must go there, he feels his body tighten long before he arrives. He scans the road, the ditches, the tree line. The sound of a truck slowing nearby makes his stomach drop. He grips tools so tightly that his hands ache. He tells himself to act normal, but his mind runs ahead to escape routes, weapons, who might be watching. He is embarrassed by his fear, especially because he has spent his life seeing himself as a strong man.

At home, his wife experiences him as present but absent. He sits through dinner without hearing whole conversations. When family members speak loudly or argue, he becomes visibly tense and either snaps at them or leaves the room. He used to enjoy sitting outside in the evening with tea, but now he prefers to remain indoors with curtains drawn. Crowded gatherings at weddings, the market, and even the mosque become difficult. He watches entrances, flinches when men brush past him, and feels anger rise quickly if someone stands too close. He has begun declining invitations, telling relatives he is tired or busy with the farm.

What troubles him most is how much the assault has changed his sense of himself. He replays the event while working, asking why he did not see danger sooner, why he could not fight them off, whether he did something to invite it. He feels shame when he catches his wife looking at him with worry. He is more irritable with her than he wants to be, then withdraws in guilt. On some mornings he sits in the truck for several minutes before turning the key, already exhausted by the day ahead. He says the world no longer feels ordered. A field he has walked for decades can suddenly feel hostile. The ordinary sounds of farm life—metal clanging, tires on gravel, voices carried across open land—arrive in his body as warnings.

Months later, the bruises are long gone, but he continues to live as though the assault is still unfolding just beyond sight. He works, because work is what he knows, but every task now happens alongside vigilance. He loves his wife and remains committed to his family, yet he feels cut off from them by something he cannot fully explain. He says he used to feel at home on his land. Now he feels as if he is guarding it, and himself, every hour he is awake.
